The study is of exploratory and non-causal nature.

rationale: This observational (explicitly exploratory and non-causal) quantitative study models data from 1,215 households (Model 1) and 254 functional handpump user groups (Model 2) in Kwale County, Kenya to examine institutional pluralism and uptake of a delegated, performance-based maintenance contract with a professional service provider (FundiFix Ltd). The primary mechanism family is regulatory_model_ownership (comparing community, private/individualist, and public/bureaucratic management models and delegated professional maintenance contracting), while assigned_mechanism_label_with_multiple is 'multiple' because the regressions co-equally test fees_tariffs_subsidies (pre-existing regular payment rules, subsidized monthly maintenance tariffs, and fee remissions for vulnerable users—the main statistically significant institutional predictors), participation_assistance (water user committee composition and club rules), and enforcement_sanctions (penalties for non-payment and exclusion for rule violations), alongside broader discussion of devolution (institutional_structure_coordination). Both empirical dependent variables—household 'intent to contract' and user-group 'contract commitment'—are institutional/governance uptake intermediate outcomes (administrative_outcome), whereas reliability, water quality, distance, and cost perceptions enter as explanatory predictors rather than modeled outcomes.
